Polytheism is the belief in, and often the worship of, multiple gods — not just one, but many. That's really the heart of it.

In a polytheistic worldview, the universe is not governed by a single all-powerful God, but by many gods, each of whom is a distinct being with their own personality, powers, desires, and flaws. These gods are not just vague spiritual forces — they are more like powerful individuals who can think, feel, argue, fall in love, get jealous, and make decisions.

Each god typically has a specific domain — an area of life or nature that they rule over or represent. For example, one god might control the sea, another might govern war, another might be in charge of love, harvest, death, the sun, wisdom, and so on. The gods are specialists, in a sense.
How these gods relate to each other

In most polytheistic traditions, the gods don't exist in isolation. They form a community — they interact, cooperate, compete, and conflict with one another. They often have family relationships: parents and children, brothers and sisters, husbands and wives. They have alliances and rivalries. They have favorites among humans and enemies among themselves. Think of them less like distant, unreachable forces, and more like a society of extraordinarily powerful beings living in their own divine world while also being deeply involved in human affairs.

There is usually some form of hierarchy among the gods too — one god might be the king or ruler of the others, the most powerful among them, while others are lesser in power. But even the lesser gods are still genuinely divine and worthy of worship.

Because there are many gods, people in polytheistic traditions don't usually feel obligated to worship all of the gods all the time. A farmer might pray mostly to the god of rain and harvest. A sailor would pray to the god of the sea. A warrior going into battle would call on the god of war. You could also have a personal favorite god — a deity you felt a special connection to — and devote most of your worship to that one, while still acknowledging the others exist.

This means polytheistic religion tends to be flexible and pluralistic. Different cities, regions, families, and professions might favor different gods, hold different festivals, or build temples to different deities — all within the same broader religious tradition.

Some of the most famous polytheistic traditions in history include:

  • Ancient Greek religion — with gods like Zeus (king of the gods, ruler of the sky), Poseidon (sea), Hades (underworld), Athena (wisdom and war strategy), Apollo (sun, music, prophecy), Aphrodite (love), Ares (war), Demeter (harvest), and many others.
  • Ancient Roman religion — very similar to Greek religion; the Romans adopted most of the Greek gods but gave them different names (Jupiter, Neptune, Minerva, Venus, Mars, etc.).
  • Norse religion — with gods like Odin (wisdom, death, war), Thor (thunder and strength), Freya (love and fertility), Loki (trickery), and others.
  • Ancient Egyptian religion — with gods like Ra (sun), Osiris (death and resurrection), Isis (magic and motherhood), Anubis (the dead and embalming), Horus (sky and kingship), and many more.
  • Mesopotamian religion (ancient Babylon and Sumer) — with gods like Marduk, Enlil, Ishtar, Ea, and others.
  • Hinduism — this is a complex case. Many Hindus worship multiple gods such as Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva, Lakshmi, Durga, Ganesha, and Saraswati. However, some Hindu philosophical traditions hold that all these gods are expressions or aspects of one ultimate reality — so whether Hinduism is strictly polytheistic is a matter of debate among scholars and Hindus themselves.
  • Shinto (Japan's traditional religion) — involves belief in kami, which are spirits or gods that inhabit natural things and places. There are thousands of kami.

For most of human history, polytheism was the dominant form of religious belief worldwide. Ancient civilizations — Mesopotamia, Egypt, Greece, Rome, India, China, the pre-Columbian Americas, northern Europe, sub-Saharan Africa — nearly all had rich polytheistic traditions. Monotheism (the belief in only one God) became widely dominant only with the rise and spread of Judaism, Christianity, and Islam over the past few thousand years. Before that, worshipping many gods was simply the default way most humans understood the divine.

Yes, very much so. Polytheism is not just something from the ancient past. It is alive and practiced today:

  • Hinduism, with hundreds of millions of followers, is still practiced worldwide.
  • Shinto is still practiced in Japan.
  • Various African traditional religions and Indigenous spiritual traditions around the world involve multiple divine beings or spirits.
  • There are also modern reconstructionist movements — groups of people who have deliberately revived ancient polytheistic traditions, such as Hellenism (revived Greek religion), Ásatrú (revived Norse religion), and others.
  • Wicca and various forms of modern paganism often involve polytheistic elements.
How polytheism compares to related ideas

It helps to place polytheism alongside a few related concepts:

  • Monotheism — belief in one God who is typically all-powerful, all-knowing, and the creator of everything. Christianity, Islam, and Judaism are monotheistic.
  • Henotheism — belief in and worship of one god as your primary god, while still acknowledging that other gods exist and are real. It's a middle ground between polytheism and monotheism.
  • Atheism — disbelief in any gods at all.
  • Pantheism — the idea that God is the universe itself, or that everything in existence is part of one divine whole — not multiple separate gods.
  • Animism — the belief that spirits or a spiritual essence inhabit natural objects, animals, and places. It's not exactly polytheism, but it shares the idea of many spiritual beings in the world.

If you had to capture polytheism in one sentence: it is the belief that divine power is not concentrated in one being, but is distributed among many gods, each real, each distinct, each with their own personality and domain, and each potentially worthy of worship. It sees the divine not as a single, unified entity, but as a whole society of powerful beings — much like humans live in communities, the gods do too, just on an incomparably grander scale.
